headline: Ph.D. Candidate at Nanyang Technological University
summary: I am a final-year PhD candidate in Computer Science at Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore. My research focuses on building efficient onboard computing systems that enable robots to understand where they are and navigate autonomously using visual perception, particularly in environments where GPS is unavailable or unreliable, such as indoor spaces, dense urban environments, underground settings, and extraterrestrial exploration.

My work sits at the intersection of computer vision, robotics, computer architecture, and hardware-software co-design. During my PhD, I have focused on developing computationally efficient Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (V-SLAM) systems using Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms. By combining algorithmic optimization, specialized hardware acceleration, and heterogeneous computing, my research aims to make real-time visual localization and perception practical for robotic systems operating under strict computational, power, and energy constraints.

As part of this work, I demonstrated a complete V-SLAM system capable of operating in real time at approximately 20 FPS within a power budget of around 5 W on an FPGA-based SoC platform. The system achieved substantially lower power consumption than embedded GPU-based implementations operating in the 10–15 W range, while delivering considerably higher processing throughput than an embedded quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 CPU implementation operating below 8 FPS. These results highlight the potential of FPGA-based SoCs as flexible, and energy-efficient computing platforms for resource-constrained autonomous systems.

Building on this foundation, my broader research direction is collaborative localization and autonomy. I am interested in enabling teams of robots to share observations, build a common understanding of their surroundings, and determine their locations accurately and efficiently through distributed perception and computation. Such capabilities are important for applications including robot and drone swarms, cooperative exploration, autonomous inspection and monitoring, and multi-robot systems operating in complex or previously unknown environments.

More broadly, I am interested in designing efficient computing architectures, including specialized hardware and deep learning accelerators, that bring increasingly capable intelligence directly onto edge devices. Beyond autonomous robotics, these ideas are also relevant to emerging applications such as Augmented Reality (AR) and Mixed Reality (MR), where accurate, low-latency visual perception and localization must be performed continuously under tight computational and energy constraints.
research: My current research helps a robot estimate its position and build a map using cameras, a process known as visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). I design the algorithms and the computing hardware together, using reconfigurable chips called FPGAs to make demanding vision tasks faster and more energy efficient.

This work provides a foundation for robots that can share spatial information and act together. I aim to support practical applications such as precision agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and environmental monitoring.
